references.text: Repeats the prohibition against oppressing foreigners and reminds that the Israelites themselves were foreigners in Egypt, emphasizing that they know the foreigner's soul.
Expands the command to treat foreigners well by requiring that they be loved as oneself, with the same reasoning regarding Israel's stay in Egypt.
Commands Israel to love the foreigner because they themselves were foreigners in Egypt, and links this to God's own love for foreigners.
Prohibits perverting justice for foreigners and fatherless children, reminding of slavery in Egypt as the basis for fair treatment.
Declares a curse on anyone who perverts justice for foreigners, widows, and fatherless children.
The prophet Jeremiah warns against oppressing foreigners, fatherless children, and widows, in connection with a call to repentance.
Ezekiel accuses Jerusalem of treating foreigners with violence and oppression, as a violation of this commandment.
The people of the land are accused of oppressing foreigners without justice, as part of Ezekiel's judgment against Israel.
Zechariah conveys the Lord's word not to oppress widows, fatherless children, foreigners, or the poor.
The Lord testifies against those who oppress foreigners and do not fear Him, in Malachi's prophecy about judgment.
The exhortation to hospitality toward foreigners in Hebrews builds on the Old Testament tradition of welcoming strangers.
Uses the same historical memory of foreignness to justify a specific prohibition against hatred.
A direct parallel in the law that forbids oppressing immigrants with the same underlying ethics.
